Family Health

Colorectal cancer: symptoms, stages, tests and treatment

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Colorectal cancer begins in the colon or rectum, the lower parts of the digestive tract. It is a common cancer, but an individual’s risk and outlook cannot be read from a population statistic alone. Some people have no noticeable symptoms at diagnosis. Others develop changes that can also occur with less serious conditions. Tests establish what is happening; the location, extent and biology of a confirmed cancer help guide treatment.

What colorectal cancer means

The colon makes up most of the large bowel, and the rectum is the section near its end. Cancer that starts in the colon is called colon cancer; cancer starting in the rectum is rectal cancer. The term colorectal cancer covers both, although their treatment plans are not always identical.

Cancer develops when changes in cells allow them to grow in an uncontrolled way. A tumour can grow into nearby tissue and may spread through blood or lymphatic channels to other parts of the body. That spread is called metastasis.

Many colorectal cancers develop from certain types of growths called polyps. Not every polyp is cancer, and not every polyp will become cancer. Its type and microscopic features help determine the risk and the follow-up needed. Finding and removing suitable precancerous polyps can prevent some cancers.

What the stages describe

Staging describes how far a cancer has grown or spread. It helps the team discuss treatment and prognosis. It is established from findings such as scans, biopsies and examination of tissue removed during surgery: not from the number or severity of symptoms.

Stage 0, also called carcinoma in situ, means abnormal or cancerous cells are confined to the innermost lining. They have not invaded deeper bowel-wall tissue.

Stage I means the cancer has grown into deeper layers of the bowel wall, potentially reaching the muscle layer, without spread to regional lymph nodes or distant sites.

Stage II means the cancer has grown farther through the wall and may involve nearby structures, but without regional lymph-node involvement or distant metastases.

Stage III involves regional lymph nodes or specified tumour deposits in nearby tissue, without distant spread. It is not synonymous with terminal illness.

Stage IV means cancer has spread to distant sites, such as the liver, lungs or distant lymph nodes, or has spread on the lining of the abdominal cavity. The distribution of that spread matters when treatment is considered.

These are broad groupings. The TNM system records the primary tumour, regional nodes and metastases in more detail, and some numbered stages have subgroups. The stage estimated before surgery can be refined by the pathology results afterwards.

Symptoms that deserve assessment

Possible bowel symptoms include a persistent change from your usual pattern, such as constipation, diarrhea, narrower stools or a feeling that the bowel has not emptied fully. Blood may be visible in the stool or there may be bleeding from the rectum.

Abdominal pain, cramps, bloating or frequent gas can also occur. Unexplained weight loss, weakness and unusual tiredness deserve attention, particularly when they accompany other changes. Blood loss can contribute to anemia, which may add to fatigue.

These symptoms do not automatically mean cancer. Hemorrhoids, infection and other bowel conditions can produce overlapping symptoms. However, repeatedly assuming that a change is harmless can delay an appropriate assessment.

Tell a clinician about persistent or unexplained symptoms, and seek prompt advice about bleeding. Do not wait until you reach a screening age, or wait a fixed month because a symptom list assigns that duration to a particular stage. Younger adults can also develop colorectal cancer.

Why symptoms cannot tell you the stage

Constipation is not a marker of stage I, and weight loss does not establish stage III. A cancer may cause symptoms relatively early because of its location, while another may grow without obvious warning signs. A symptom-by-stage table can therefore be misleading.

Advanced disease may produce symptoms related to the organs affected. For example, liver involvement can sometimes be associated with jaundice, and disease involving the lungs can cause respiratory symptoms. Swelling, bone pain or neurological symptoms require assessment but are not diagnostic evidence of metastasis by themselves.

Persistent headache, blurred vision or a fracture should not be interpreted from an article as proof of stage IV colorectal cancer. These problems have other possible causes. Likewise, their absence cannot exclude advanced disease.

Severe abdominal pain with vomiting, swelling and inability to pass stool or gas may indicate an obstruction and needs urgent assessment. Heavy bleeding, fainting or sudden breathing difficulty also requires urgent help rather than a routine screening appointment.

Screening and investigating symptoms are different

Screening looks for cancer or precancerous changes in people who do not have symptoms. Investigating a new bowel change or rectal bleeding is a diagnostic process. A person with symptoms should not be told simply to wait for their next routine screening invitation.

Screening ages, tests and intervals vary by country and by risk. In the United States, major recommendations start routine average-risk screening at age 45, usually continuing through 75, with decisions later in life individualized. A significant family history, inherited syndrome or other high-risk history may require an earlier and different schedule.

A clinician begins by asking about symptoms, previous bowel conditions and family history. An examination may include the abdomen and, when appropriate, a gloved-finger examination of the rectum. Neither a normal abdominal examination nor a normal rectal examination excludes a tumour elsewhere in the bowel.

Stool tests: guaiac, FIT and home collection

Stool tests can look for blood that is too small to see. A guaiac-based fecal occult blood test uses a chemical reaction that changes colour when blood is detected. The instructions may include dietary or medication precautions. Follow the particular kit’s directions and do not stop prescribed medicine on your own.

A fecal immunochemical test, usually called FIT, uses antibodies to detect human hemoglobin. It is designed to detect bleeding from the lower bowel and generally does not require the same food restrictions as a guaiac test. A positive result does not identify cancer as the cause; other conditions can bleed too.

Home collection means that you collect the sample outside a clinic, often before returning it for laboratory analysis. The number of samples, storage instructions and return process depend on the test. There is no universal promise of a result in five minutes or five working days.

Follow the kit instructions and find out who will review the result. An abnormal screening stool test usually needs a colonoscopy. A negative result does not remove the need to assess persistent symptoms.

Some screening programmes also use stool tests that combine blood detection with DNA or RNA markers. These are not all interchangeable with a simple over-the-counter blood test. Ask which test is appropriate and what follow-up it requires.

Blood tests and endoscopic examinations

Routine blood tests can help identify anemia and assess liver function or other aspects of health. They may contribute to an investigation but do not, by themselves, confirm or exclude colorectal cancer. Special blood-based screening tests are a separate category; their role depends on current recommendations and does not replace diagnostic assessment of symptoms.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy uses a slender viewing instrument to examine the rectum and lower colon. It can identify abnormal tissue and allow sampling, but it does not inspect the whole colon.

Colonoscopy examines the colon and rectum with a flexible camera instrument. It can be used as a screening test or as part of investigating symptoms or another abnormal result. The clinician can often remove polyps or take small tissue samples during the procedure.

Those samples are examined in a laboratory. The pathology report helps establish whether cancer is present and what type it is. It may also provide information important for treatment or inherited-risk assessment.

Examples of screening schedules for eligible average-risk people include a yearly FIT or a colonoscopy every ten years, with other intervals for other tests. Those intervals do not apply automatically after an abnormal finding, with symptoms, or for someone at increased risk.

Imaging and the difference between CT scans

CT colonography, sometimes called virtual colonoscopy, uses CT images to examine the bowel. It can show polyps or other abnormalities, but it cannot take a biopsy or remove a polyp. A concerning result may therefore lead to a conventional colonoscopy.

A CT scan used to look for spread in the chest, abdomen or pelvis has a different purpose. Not every CT scan for colorectal cancer is a virtual colonoscopy. Additional imaging, such as MRI in a rectal-cancer assessment, may be used according to the clinical question.

Older descriptions of bowel investigation may mention a barium enema followed by X-rays. Barium is a contrast material that helps outline the bowel; it is not itself radioactive. This examination is no longer a standard first choice in many modern pathways. The clinician should explain why a particular test is being recommended.

Different tumour types

Most colorectal cancers are adenocarcinomas, arising from glandular cells in the bowel lining. Knowing the precise type matters because a less common tumour can require a different approach.

Other tumours that can occur in or affect the bowel include neuroendocrine tumours, historically often called carcinoids; lymphomas arising from immune cells; and sarcomas involving supporting tissues such as muscle or blood vessels.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumours, or GISTs, are another distinct group and are much more often found outside the colon, such as in the stomach or small intestine. Their behaviour is assessed using their own features. They should not be described simply as ordinary benign polyps that inevitably turn into colorectal adenocarcinoma.

Ask the team to explain the pathology diagnosis. Information written for the common adenocarcinoma may not apply in the same way to every tumour found in the large bowel.

Causes and risk factors

Changes in genes controlling cell behaviour can be acquired during life or, in some cases, inherited. An inherited predisposition raises risk but is not the same as a guarantee that cancer will develop. Some cancers occur without an obvious inherited explanation.

Risk is influenced by age, a personal history of colorectal cancer or certain polyps, a family history of the disease and inherited conditions such as Lynch syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis. Longstanding inflammatory bowel disease, particularly colitis, can also affect surveillance needs.

Risk generally rises with age, but being younger than fifty does not provide immunity. Differences reported between population groups also need context: ancestry, inherited variants, access to screening and other social and health factors should not be reduced to a diagnosis based on ethnicity.

Smoking, alcohol use, excess body weight, physical inactivity and diets high in processed meat are associated with increased risk. Type 2 diabetes is also associated with colorectal cancer risk, but it should not be labelled as something every individual could simply have prevented.

Appropriate screening and changes to modifiable risks can reduce the chance of cancer, but they cannot provide complete protection. A diagnosis is not proof that someone caused their illness through a particular food or lifestyle choice.

Surgery and the possibility of a stoma

Treatment depends on the tumour’s location, stage, pathology and the person’s health and preferences. Some very early cancers can be removed during an endoscopic procedure. The tissue findings determine whether that removal is sufficient; the mere fact that a cancer was found in a polyp does not settle the question.

A larger or more deeply invasive tumour may require removal of a segment of colon or rectum and nearby lymph nodes. The remaining bowel may be joined together in an operation called an anastomosis.

Sometimes stool needs to leave through an opening in the abdominal wall called a stoma. A colostomy uses the colon; some operations instead involve an ileostomy from the small bowel. The stoma may be temporary or permanent, depending on the operation and subsequent recovery.

Ask before surgery whether a stoma is possible, what would determine its duration and who will teach you to care for it. The operation and postoperative pathology also help the team decide whether additional treatment is needed.

Chemotherapy and radiation treatment

Chemotherapy uses medicines to kill cancer cells or limit their growth. Depending on the cancer, it may be used after surgery to reduce recurrence risk, before another treatment, or to help control disease that has spread. It is not automatically necessary for every early cancer.

Medicines used in colorectal-cancer regimens include fluorouracil, also called 5-FU, capecitabine, oxaliplatin and irinotecan. They may be combined in different ways. A drug name on a list is not a recommendation for a particular patient or a guide to the dose.

Ask about likely side effects, how they can be managed and what symptoms require an immediate call. Supportive medicines may help, but not every side effect should be managed by adding another medicine without assessment.

Radiotherapy directs radiation at a treatment area. It is used more routinely in some rectal-cancer pathways than in colon-cancer treatment and may be combined with medicines. Its timing and purpose depend on the site and stage. The terms colon and rectal cancer should not be treated as if they always imply the same sequence of care.

Targeted treatment and immunotherapy

Targeted medicines act on particular pathways involved in cancer growth. Examples used in selected colorectal-cancer situations include bevacizumab, ramucirumab, ziv-aflibercept, cetuximab, panitumumab and regorafenib. This is not a complete list, and the medicines are not interchangeable.

Immunotherapy helps the immune system act against cancer. Pembrolizumab, nivolumab and ipilimumab have roles in particular settings. The tumour’s molecular characteristics, including mismatch repair deficiency or high microsatellite instability, can be central to whether an immune treatment is appropriate.

These treatments are not all reserved for a final stage after every other option has failed. For example, current United States approval includes nivolumab with ipilimumab for unresectable or metastatic MSI-H or dMMR colorectal cancer. That does not mean the combination is suitable for every colorectal tumour.

Treatment availability and approved uses vary by country and change over time. Ask which biomarker tests have been done, what the proposed medicine is intended to achieve and why it is appropriate for your specific cancer.

Possible complications after surgery

Bowel surgery carries risks, including reactions to anesthesia, bleeding, infection and blood clots. The surgeon should explain the risks most relevant to the planned procedure and your health.

Other possible complications include leakage from a bowel join, an abnormal connection called a fistula, injury to nearby structures such as the bladder or urinary tract, and adhesions that can contribute to bowel obstruction. A hernia can develop at an incision site. These are possibilities to discuss, not outcomes that everyone will experience.

Before discharge, know which symptoms need a call to the surgical team and which require emergency care. Increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, wound changes, chest symptoms or problems with a stoma should be reported according to the discharge plan. Do not assume that every new symptom is simply part of normal recovery.

Recovering after colorectal surgery

Hospital stay depends on the operation, bowel function, ability to eat and drink, mobility and any complications. A fixed promise of three or four days will not fit every patient. Ask what milestones the team uses to decide that you can go home safely.

Enhanced-recovery programmes commonly encourage getting out of bed and taking supported walks early after surgery. Waiting three weeks before any walking is not a general rule. Increase activity as the team advises and ask how to manage stairs safely.

Lifting, driving and sexual activity need separate advice. There is no universal four-kilogram limit or single date that applies to every operation. Driving also depends on pain, the ability to respond safely and any medicine that affects alertness.

Follow the wound-care instructions you are given, including when showering is allowed. Do not assume that every surgical wound must be kept completely away from water until a later visit.

Eating and drinking may need adjustment as the bowel recovers. Follow the diet and fluid plan, particularly if you have a stoma or another condition that affects fluid balance. An instruction to drink eight to ten glasses each day cannot replace an individualized plan.

Take medicines as prescribed and ask about constipation, diarrhea or painful straining. Keep the follow-up appointment and the team’s contact details available. Recovery may take longer than expected, and a change in progress is a reason to ask for advice.

Understanding survival statistics and prognosis

A cancer diagnosis can be frightening, and population statistics can be difficult to interpret. Five-year relative survival compares survival in people with a particular cancer group with survival expected in a comparable general population. It is not a time limit or an individual prediction.

The American Cancer Society’s January 2026 page reports United States data for people diagnosed in 2014–2020. For colon cancer, five-year relative survival is about 91 percent for localized disease, 74 percent for regional disease and 13 percent for distant disease. For rectal cancer, the corresponding figures are about 90, 74 and 18 percent.

These broad SEER groups are not interchangeable with numbered TNM stages. They describe extent at initial diagnosis and should not be used as a forecast for someone whose cancer later recurs. Treatments also change after the period in which a dataset was collected.

The outlook for an individual depends on more than a group percentage. Where the disease is, whether it can be fully removed, tumour biology, bowel obstruction or perforation, general health, previous treatment and response to therapy can all matter.

Ask the treating team how it interprets the information in your situation and what the next treatment or follow-up decision involves. A stage number or a table found online cannot replace that discussion.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

National Cancer Institute guidance separates diagnosis, anatomical staging and treatment selection. A bowel symptom list cannot establish the presence or stage of cancer.

Screening recommendations apply to defined groups without symptoms. Abnormal screening results need follow-up, while symptoms and increased-risk histories require their own assessment pathway.

How BeMama can help

BeMama provides general health education that can help families understand terms and prepare questions for an appointment. It is not a colorectal-cancer screening service and cannot interpret a biopsy, assign a cancer stage or select treatment.

When to seek help

Seek medical assessment for persistent or unexplained bowel changes or rectal bleeding. Heavy bleeding, fainting, severe abdominal pain with vomiting or inability to pass stool or gas needs urgent help. After surgery or during cancer treatment, follow the team’s emergency-contact instructions.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Colorectal cancer may be present without obvious symptoms; persistent changes deserve assessment.
  • Symptoms do not determine the stage. Staging uses anatomical and pathology findings.
  • Screening tests and tests for symptoms have different purposes and follow-up requirements.
  • The site, tumour type, stage and biomarkers influence treatment options.
  • Surgical recovery should follow an individual plan, commonly including early supported movement.
  • Survival percentages describe populations and are not a personal deadline.

Frequently asked questions

Can thin stools or fatigue tell me my cancer stage?

No. Those symptoms can have several causes and cannot identify a stage. Examination, imaging and pathology establish the extent of a confirmed cancer.

Does a positive FIT mean I definitely have cancer?

No. It detects blood, which can have other causes. It does require the recommended follow-up, usually colonoscopy.

Do I need to wait until screening age if I have bleeding?

No. New or unexplained symptoms require assessment independently of a routine screening schedule.

Is every CT scan a virtual colonoscopy?

No. CT colonography examines the bowel in a particular way; other CT scans may be used to assess spread or another clinical question.

Will surgery always mean a permanent stoma?

No. Some operations need no stoma, some need a temporary one, and others a permanent one. Ask what is possible with your operation.

Is immunotherapy appropriate for everyone?

No. Tumour characteristics, approved uses and clinical circumstances determine whether it is suitable.

Does five-year survival mean that people live for only five years?

No. It is a statistical comparison at a specified time point, not a limit on how long someone may live.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
